Subject: Outbound controls for private gateway: questions before infra kick-off

Diego —

We’re finalizing the networking work for the private deployment in our us-west-2 VPC and I wanted to confirm Redwood’s expectations for outbound connectivity so we can map firewall rules and schedule a connectivity test. A few quick questions: 

1) Do you require static egress IPs per customer, or can we SNAT to a shared NAT pool?
2) Which hostnames/FQDNs and IP ranges should be allowlisted for the control plane, metrics, and pull/push endpoints?
3) Any preference on TLS interception / proxy behavior (we run a decrypting TLS proxy for traffic inspection)?
4) What telemetry do you expect from our side (flow logs, connection timestamps, client certs)?

We need this info before we approve the firewall rules with our security/compliance team. If you have a short checklist or diagram, that would help.

Thanks — happy to hop on a call tomorrow.

Alice —

Thanks for the clear list. I’m looping in Irene (security) and Michael (infra) to provide our recommended policy and a short checklist. High level answers now:

- We prefer static, customer-dedicated egress IPs when customers need a strict allowlist for the control plane or have regulatory requirements. If you can’t dedicate an IP per customer we can accept a stable NAT pool per-region, but we’ll need the exact NAT IPs before production.
- Primary outbound is HTTPS (443) to our control endpoints and metrics; we will provide FQDNs and regional CIDRs.
- We strongly prefer NO TLS MITM for control-plane connections — see security note below.
- Telemetry: flow logs and timestamped connection records help, and we can accept signed connection attestations (mTLS) for higher assurance.

I’m attaching a lightweight checklist + diagram (initial). Irene/Michael — could you expand with specific CIDRs, port list, and any network config snippets (SNAT/NAT gateway, route table, DNS behavior) we should give Acme?

Hi all —

Quick security-oriented summary and requirements for private endpoints / egress controls. I’ve kept this concise so Acme can drop items into their firewall change request.

Design recommendations (high level):
- Dedicated egress path: prefer a dedicated NAT gateway or small set of static IPs per-customer for control-plane and telemetry traffic. This minimizes blast radius and eases allowlisting.
- Split traffic by purpose: control-plane & metrics (Redwood) vs. OS/patching/registry pulls. Use route tables or proxy policies to segregate these flows.
- DNS: use split-horizon (private DNS) so private endpoints resolve to internal IPs; if external resolver is used ensure DNS over TLS (DoT) to avoid poisoning.
- TLS interception: control-plane connections MUST be exempt from TLS interception / decryption. We authenticate servers by certificate pins and require end-to-end TLS for integrity. If your security team insists on inspection, we can provide public-key or certificate fingerprint information for exception rules.

Minimal allowlist and ports (control-plane & telemetry):
- Destination: FQDNs: api.redwood-inference.com, control-metrics.redwood-inference.com, auth.redwood-inference.com (we’ll provide region-specific aliases)
- Preferred: allow by FQDN + SNI, and secondarily by destination CIDR ranges. Example region-US egress pool: 52.33.120.0/24, 52.33.121.0/24 (we will provide final ranges in the doc).
- Ports/protocols: TCP 443 (HTTPS, required), UDP 123 (NTP, if you run time sync externally), TCP 80 allowed only for OS registries if necessary but behind a proxy.

Operational & compliance controls: 
- Flow logs: export VPC flow logs and share a daily digest (or give us read access to the log bucket) during onboarding tests.
- Connection metadata: timestamps, source IP (post-SNAT), destination FQDN, and TLS SNI are helpful. We can accept mTLS client certs for additional authentication.
- Retention: keep logs for 90 days at minimum during onboarding; longer-term retention is negotiable for audits.

Testing & cutover:
- Connectivity test: we’ll need a stable egress IP for a week to validate allowlists. Please designate a single NAT IP or a small range for the test window.
- Fallback: if a per-customer IP is not available, configure NAT mapping with a strong session affinity and share the mapping table during the test.

I’ll attach the checklist and a small diagram. Diego — flag me if Acme needs mTLS certs or a CA fingerprint; we can provide details out-of-band.

Irene Choi
Head of Security & Trust
Redwood Inference

From: Michael Grant <michael_grant@redwood.example.com>

Subject: Re: Outbound controls for private gateway: questions before infra kick-off

Hello —

Adding concrete configuration guidance for your network team. These are examples — replace CIDRs/IPs with your assigned addresses.

1) NAT strategy
- Preferred: Per-customer NAT gateway with one or two static Elastic IPs (EIP). Advertise these to Acme’s allowlist.
- Alternative: Regional NAT pool with long-lived mappings. If using pool, enable session affinity and provide mapping snapshots.

2) Firewall rules (example):
- Allow: dst 52.33.120.0/24, 52.33.121.0/24 tcp 443 (Redwood control plane and metrics)
- Allow: dst registry-1.docker.io tcp 443 (for image pulls) — constrain to build subnets if possible
- Allow (optional): dst 0.0.0.0/0 udp 123 (NTP) if hosts use external NTP; better to point hosts to internal NTP server
- Deny: outbound tcp 22 from production subnets to reduce exfil risk (except for jump-boxes)

3) DNS handling
- Route control-plane hostnames via your private DNS zone to internal VIPs when behind the private endpoint. If you cannot, use DNS over TLS (port 853) to a trusted resolver.

4) Sample iptables-style SNAT rule (linux NAT gateway):
- iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 10.10.0.0/16 -o eth0 -j SNAT --to-source 54.200.12.45

5) Observability hooks
- Push flow logs to our onboarding bucket (s3://redwood-onboard/acme/flows) or grant read-only. Include connection start/end times, source post-SNAT IP, dest IP, dest port, and TLS SNI if available.

If you want, we can provide a short runbook for the connectivity test (what endpoints to curl, expected TLS fingerprint, how to capture curl --trace).

Michael Grant
Infrastructure Engineering
Redwood Inference
